item.title: Salman Muqtadir studio vandalism: Three accused sent to jail
item.description:
A Dhaka court on Sunday sent 3 accused to jail in a case filed over trespassing, vandalism, looting and theft at content creator Salman Muqtadir’s Brownfish Studio in the capital.
Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Arifur Rahman passed the order after Inspector Subrata Debnath, the investigating officer of the case, produced the accused before the court and sought a 5-day remand. The court fixed Wednesday for a hearing on the remand plea.
Sub-Inspector Tarekur Rahman of the prosecution department confirmed the information.
The accused are Md Mamun, 32, Md Aslam, 24, and Munna, 29.
According to the case statement, around 50 people formed an unlawful assembly and trespassed into the project area of New Gini Properties Ltd in West Matikata under Cantonment police station on Saturday.
They allegedly fired around 50 rounds indiscriminately and attacked people with ramdas, knives and sticks. Several people, including site engineer Md Parvez, were seriously injured.
The attackers also trespassed into Salman Muqtadir’s Brownfish Studio and vandalized and looted the premises.
The case statement said the attackers took away cash, laptops, computers, BRB cables, cameras and professional media equipment from the project area. Several vehicles were also vandalized.
The company suffered losses of around Tk 1 crore 42 lakh 80,000, while goods worth Tk 1 crore 50 lakh 44,000 were stolen, according to the case statement.
After receiving information about the incident, police from Cantonment Police Station went to the scene. The attackers allegedly fired at the police, who fired 5 shotgun rounds in self-defense to bring the situation under control.
Two accused named in the case were arrested at the scene, while another was arrested later during a police drive.
Police said locally made weapons and empty bullet casings were recovered from the arrested suspects.
Saiful Islam Bhuiyan, an official of the project, filed the case with Cantonment police station.
The case names 10 people as accused and includes another 150–200 unidentified people.

item.title: UICC World Cancer Congress concludes with call for greater investment and equity in cancer care
item.description:
The World Cancer Congress 2026 concluded on Saturday with calls for stronger global collaboration, increased investment in cancer infrastructure and broader access to care, particularly in low- and middle-income countries where demand is rising and families face significant financial burdens.
More than 2,000 delegates from over 120 countries attended the three-day Congress, organized by the Union for International Cancer Control (UICC) and hosted by the Hong Kong Anti-Cancer Society.
The closing session highlighted a central challenge: translating advances in cancer science into accessible and affordable care.
UICC President-elect Zainab Shinkafi-Bagudu said cancer centers in low- and middle-income countries are facing increasing demand, with families often paying out of pocket for treatment.
“Investment in cancer infrastructure is not optional; it’s an urgent need,” she said, emphasizing the importance of keeping patients, survivors, clinicians and advocates at the center of cancer-control planning.
She also addressed food insecurity and the challenge of producing more food with limited resources, calling for stronger measures to protect food systems and public health, particularly in lower-income countries.
Photo: Courtesy
UICC President Ulrika Årehed Kågström urged delegates to apply ideas and practical lessons from the Congress in their own countries and organizations.
Reflecting on a message she gave at the opening of the Congress to “be curious,” Årehed Kågström said the meeting brought together clinicians, researchers, advocates, survivors and policymakers, creating opportunities to exchange ideas that could be adapted to different health systems.
She acknowledged that cancer control is a complex challenge, covering prevention and early detection to treatment, supportive care and survivorship.
The 6 regional meetings held during the Congress also focused on how countries and organizations could advance the objectives of the UICC World Cancer Declaration.
The discussions broadly centered on 3 themes — collaboration, prevention and equity — including sharing expertise, strengthening prevention efforts and expanding access to services for underserved communities.
“No individual leader can address the global cancer challenge alone,” was a recurring message from the closing session, with speakers emphasizing collective action across countries and institutions.
The Congress showcased developments in precision oncology, artificial intelligence and cancer screening while highlighting the gap between scientific progress and access to care.
Elizabeth Mittendorf of the American Society of Clinical Oncology cited clinical trial evidence suggesting that targeting the RAS gene could substantially extend survival for some patients with pancreatic cancer compared with chemotherapy.
Artificial intelligence featured in discussions on cancer research, early detection, diagnosis and healthcare delivery.
The International Agency for Research on Cancer also presented evidence on lung cancer screening, highlighting findings that targeted low-dose CT screening among people at high risk can reduce lung cancer mortality and advanced-stage disease.
Breast and cervical cancer were also major areas of discussion, including early diagnosis, referral systems, patient navigation and efforts to maintain progress toward the World Health Organization’s cervical cancer elimination goals.
The closing discussions underscored that scientific advances require investment in health infrastructure and systems that can deliver them.
The Congress also examined the impact of war on cancer services, with participants from Ukraine and Gaza describing disruptions to treatment and healthcare infrastructure.
They highlighted shortages of medicines and equipment, displacement and difficulties maintaining treatment over extended periods.
The sessions stressed that cancer care needs to be included in humanitarian preparedness and response because patients requiring surgery, radiotherapy or repeated treatment cannot simply postpone care until a crisis ends.
Cancer prevention discussions also addressed the influence of tobacco, alcohol and ultra-processed food industries on public health policy.
Participants examined concerns about industry lobbying and discussed the need for greater transparency and safeguards against commercial interference in health policymaking.
They also discussed food insecurity and agricultural practices in relation to health and cancer prevention.
People affected by cancer played a prominent role throughout the Congress as speakers, advocates and participants in policy discussions.
Sessions examined how patient organizations and people with lived experience can contribute to national cancer-control planning and help ensure that policies reflect local needs.
Supportive care, palliative care and survivorship also received greater attention.
During the Congress, UICC and La Roche-Posay announced the “Mind the Gap” collaboration, which will examine disparities in supportive cancer care across health systems and identify barriers to making such care a core part of comprehensive cancer treatment.
The closing ceremony recognized organizations and individuals for contributions to cancer advocacy, research and action.
Children’s Cancer Center Lebanon, The Brunei Cancer Center and Engraced Life Foundation received the World Cancer Day 2026 Awards for their campaigns around World Cancer Day on February 4.
The Congress also recognized recipients of its Abstract Presentation and Paper Prizes, including Sarah McHutchison of the McCabe Center for Law & Cancer in Australia, Viktoriia Romaniuk of NGO Athena and Women Against Cancer in Ukraine, Cheryl Fung of the Hong Kong Anti-Cancer Society and Lu Chen of Tianjin Medical University Cancer Institute and Hospital in China.
Outgoing President Ulrika Årehed Kågström thanked delegates, speakers, volunteers, partners and the Hong Kong Anti-Cancer Society for their contributions, saying she was leaving Hong Kong exhausted but inspired by the ideas and people she had met.
The next stages of UICC’s global engagement will include the World Cancer Leaders’ Summit in Kenya, while the next World Cancer Congress is planned for Geneva, Switzerland.
As the Hong Kong Congress closed, UICC leadership emphasized that progress in cancer control will depend not only on scientific innovation but also on sustained collaboration, stronger health systems, investment and access to care.
The challenge now is to turn the ideas exchanged in Hong Kong into action in countries and communities worldwide, participants noted.

item.title: Home minister: Police negligence found in probe into Radda clinic attack
item.description:
Initial evidence of police inaction and negligence of duty has been found in connection with the attack, looting and vandalism at the Radda MCH-FP Centre, also known as Radda Clinic, in Mirpur, Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said on Sunday.
He said the officer-in-charge (OC) of Shah Ali Police Station had been withdrawn immediately and departmental proceedings were being initiated against him.
The home minister made the remarks at a press briefing on the law-and-order situation and contemporary issues at the conference room of the Ministry of Home Affairs at the Bangladesh Secretariat on Sunday afternoon.
Regarding the attack on the health centre, Salahuddin said the Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) commissioner had been instructed to inspect the scene. Following the visit, police arrested nine suspects and recovered a number of looted items and other evidence, he said.
“Strict legal action will be taken against all those involved in the incident,” the minister said.
According to a press release issued by the ministry, Salahuddin also said any attempt to deteriorate the law-and-order situation would be dealt with firmly.
He said strict action was being taken against criminals regardless of their political affiliation.
“A criminal has no political identity. A criminal is a criminal,” he said.
Regarding the regular and administrative transfer of police officers, the minister said transfer would not be the final measure if an officer was found negligent in his duties or involved in criminal activity.
“If any officer is involved in sedition or any other criminal offence, legal action is being taken against him through regular criminal cases alongside strict departmental measures,” he said.
Referring to the investigation, forensic examination, filing of a case on charges of sedition and arrest of the former officer-in-charge of Cantonment Police Station, the home minister said criminal activities within the police force would not be tolerated.

item.title: Armed group attacks, attempts to take control of Adabor building
item.description:
Some 20-25 miscreants allegedly made an attempt to seize an eight-storey building in the Shyamoli Housing area of Adabor in the capital on Saturday morning.
The group, allegedly armed with locally made weapons, attacked the house around 6:30am, repeatedly striking the main gate with machetes and other weapons. They also smashed CCTV cameras and windowpanes.
Monir Hossain, nephew of the building's owner Aminur Rahman Khan, told Dhaka Tribune on Sunday afternoon that the attackers initially opened the main gate and ordered everyone inside to leave.
“When no one came out, they threatened those inside, saying, ‘Give us money. You stay in the house but don’t pay money. Get out,’” he said.
The attackers then allegedly began hacking at the gate with machetes and attempted to enter the house. When they failed to gain entry, they vandalized the property and fled, Monir said.
He said the group later used pieces of brick to break the glass of two more windows on the second floor.
Following the attack, several tenants came downstairs and informed police. A complaint was subsequently filed over the incident.
According to Monir, the building had previously been occupied by a man named Khorshed Alam on August 17, 2024. The family filed a complaint with Adabor police, but no resolution was reached, he said. They later filed a case in court and regained possession of the house through a court order on March 12 this year.
The current owner, Aminur Rahman, is a businessman. Monir said the property had also been occupied once after August 5, 2024.
Adabor police station Officer-in-Charge Zahidul Islam told Dhaka Tribune that police had received a complaint regarding an attempt to seize the house and the display of weapons in the area.
“The matter is being investigated. Efforts are underway to arrest the accused,” he said.
He added that Aminur Rahman and Khorshed Alam had been involved in a legal dispute over the property.
“There have been incidents of counter-occupation involving this property before. We had asked both parties to come to the police station for a settlement, but they did not come,” he said.

item.title: ‘bKash Forest’ initiative launched in Khulna to support environmental protection
item.description:
A forestation program has been launched in Khulna under the ‘bKash Forest’, which enables customers to contribute to real world tree planting by growing virtual trees through their digital transactions.
Khulna City Corporation and bKash jointly inaugurated the program by planting trees at Solar Park and Linear Park in the city.
Shaikh Faridul Islam, State Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change, and Nazrul Islam Monju, administrator of Khulna City Corporation, inaugurated the program at Solar Park.
Rajib Ahmed, chief executive officer of Khulna City Corporation; Imran Ahmed, conservator of Forests, Khulna Circle; Humayun Kabir, EVP and head of the regulatory & corporate affairs department at bKash; and other senior officials were also present on the occasion.
Under the program, a total of 25,000 trees will be planted across Khulna.
Speaking as chief guest, Shaikh Faridul Islam said: “Under this joint forestation program with bKash, trees will be planted and maintained in Khulna. They are also giving due importance to selecting suitable tree species for each location and ensuring their proper care.”
Referring to the government’s plan to plant trees across the country, he added: “The ministry is working to encourage individuals and organizations to undertake tree plantation initiatives alongside the government.”
Noting that Khulna and the entire southern region of the country remain vulnerable to the impacts of climate change, Nazrul Islam Monju said the government has undertaken tree plantation programs across the country, including in coastal areas, to address environmental risks.
“The Sundarbans not only sustain our lives by providing oxygen but also protect lives and property from disasters such as cyclones and storm surges. We must therefore develop a green belt across the coastal region,” he said.
Thanking bKash on behalf of the people of Khulna for participating in the forestation program, he expressed hope that the initiative would encourage many other organizations to contribute the environmental protection.
This is the first time that a mobile financial app-based initiative for ecological protection has been introduced in the country.
Every time a user takes a low-carbon action, such as using paying utility bills, opening DPS, adding money, availing loan, recharging mobile or sending money through bKash app, will earn points called “green points.”
As users accumulate green points, a virtual sapling gradually grows into a tree within their bKash Forest in bKash app.
Once the required number of points has been earned and the virtual tree reaches maturity, bKash plants a corresponding tree in the real world. Users can subsequently view updates about the real tree through the app.
In this way, the ‘bKash Forest’ initiative will enable users to make a tangible contribution to the environment through their everyday digital transactions.

item.title: Experts: Rules for tobacco control law must be formulated without delay
item.description:
“Rules are essential to make the provisions of any law effective. Therefore, following the amendment of the tobacco control law, it is imperative that the rules be formulated at the earliest possible time,” said members of the Women’s Forums Against Tobacco.
The speakers made the remarks at a discussion meeting titled ‘Tobacco Control Amended Act 2026: Expectations and Achievements’, organized by Nari Maitree at the Bangladesh Shilpakala Academy Sunday (September 27).
The speakers also thanked the government for passing the Smoking and Tobacco Products Usage (Control) Act, 2005 (Amended 2026) during the first session of Parliament.
The meeting highlighted that Bangladesh is one of the countries with a high prevalence of tobacco use.
Among South Asian countries, Bangladesh has the highest tobacco-use prevalence at 35.3%, compared with 28.6% in India and 19.1% in Pakistan.
According to the Global Adult Tobacco Survey (GATS), 2017, approximately 37.8 million adults in Bangladesh currently use tobacco.
According to the Tobacco Atlas 2025, around 200,000 people die every year in Bangladesh from diseases caused by tobacco use, while several hundred thousand more suffer disabilities.
According to recent research by the Institute of Health Economics at the University of Dhaka, tobacco-generated government revenue amounted to approximately Tk41,000 crore in FY25.
In contrast, the annual economic cost of tobacco use including deaths, other health-related losses and environmental damage was approximately Tk87,000 crore.
In other words, the economic losses caused by tobacco use are more than twice the revenue generated from the tobacco sector.
Against this backdrop, the Smoking and Tobacco Products Usage (Control) Act, 2005 (Amended 2026) was passed on April 10, 2026.
The passage of the amended law is certainly an important step toward tobacco control.
However, the next step formulating the rules to implement the law also requires the same level of importance and priority.
Newaz Halima Arly, MP, said: “The present government is committed to protecting public health from the harmful effects of tobacco. By enacting the amended tobacco control law, the government has established the necessary policy foundation. Now, to take this initiative forward, the rules need to be formulated without delay. A committee comprising various stakeholders has already been formed to facilitate the formulation of the rules. I urge the relevant authorities to expedite the process of formulating the rules on a priority basis.”
Farida Yasmin, MP, said: “Bangladesh signed the WHO FCTC in 2003, which is the world’s first international public health treaty on tobacco control. However, all the key provisions of the FCTC have not yet been reflected in the amended tobacco control law. In particular, important areas such as protecting public health policies from the influence of the tobacco industry, regulating the contents and emissions of tobacco products, raising public awareness, and supporting tobacco cessation have not been adequately reflected in the amended law. Therefore, while formulating the rules, it is essential to take into account the obligations under the FCTC and its implementation guidelines and further strengthen the country’s tobacco control framework.”
Helen Zerin Khan, MP, said: “Some important limitations still remain in the amended tobacco control law. Issues such as regulating emerging nicotine and tobacco products, including e-cigarettes and heated tobacco products, as well as controlling the sale of single cigarette sticks and loose tobacco products, have not been adequately addressed in the law. These products, in particular, are increasing the risk of tobacco and nicotine use among young people. Similarly, the sale of single cigarette sticks makes tobacco products easily accessible to young people. Therefore, these limitations need to be given due consideration while formulating the rules, and effective measures must be ensured to protect public health.”
Salina Sultana, MP, said: “The amended law allows designated smoking areas to be maintained in public places and public transport under certain conditions. The rules must contain clear and effective provisions to ensure that tobacco companies cannot exploit this provision through various tactics.”
The meeting was chaired by Shahin Akter Dolly, executive director of Nari Maitree.
Members of the Mothers’ Forum Against Tobacco, Teachers’ Forum Against Tobacco, Women Journalists’ Forum Against Tobacco, and Youth Forum Against Tobacco were also present.
They unanimously called for the formulation of appropriate rules without delay to ensure effective implementation of the amended law and strengthen tobacco control in Bangladesh.

item.title: Pakistan, BKMEA for stronger Pak-Bangladesh textile ties
item.description:
In a bid to deepen trade collaboration and unlock supply chain synergies, High Commissioner of Pakistan Imran Haider met with Mohammad Hatem, President of the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BKMEA), at the association’s Dhaka office today.
The high-level bilateral session, attended by several BKMEA directors, focused on accelerating joint initiatives under the existing Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between BKMEA and the Pakistan Hosiery Manufacturers and Exporters Association (PHMA).
Both sides underscored the importance of organizing targeted business-to-business (B2B) meetings to bridge industry players and expand commercial avenues across both markets.
Highlighting new opportunities for cooperation, President Hatem formally invited Pakistani textile companies to participate in the upcoming Bangladesh International Textile, Knitting and Garment Industry Exhibition, slated for January 2027 in Dhaka.
The event is expected to serve as a key platform for deepening cross-border industrial integration.
High Commissioner Haider reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to facilitating seamless trade partnerships, assuring the BKMEA leadership of full support to expand commercial engagement and build a more robust bilateral trading environment.

item.title: Ershad Shikder’s convicted aide arrested after 27 years
item.description:
Zainal Sardar, a convicted associate of executed criminal Ershad Shikder, has been arrested in Khulna after 27 years in hiding.
Zainal, who was sentenced to life imprisonment in a murder case filed with Rupsha Police Station in Khulna, was arrested during a joint operation by teams from SRB-6 and SRB-8 in the Sonadanga area of Khulna city.
Lt Colonel Nistar Ahmed, commander of SRB-6, confirmed the arrest.
He said the joint teams from the headquarters companies of SRB-6 and SRB-8 conducted the operation at around 10:50pm on Saturday based on intelligence and information obtained through technology.
Zainal Sardar is the son of the late Ahammad Ali Sardar of Bongkura village under Gournadi police station in Barisal district.
According to case records, Zainal was convicted in a murder case filed with Rupsha Police Station in 1999. The court sentenced him to life imprisonment with hard labour and fined him Tk10,000. In default of payment, he was ordered to serve an additional one year in simple imprisonment.
The court also sentenced him to five years of rigorous imprisonment and fined him Tk5,000 for concealing the victim’s body. In default of payment, he was ordered to serve an additional six months in simple imprisonment.
Zainal remained absconding for years following the court’s verdict and was eventually arrested after 27 years.
The arrested convict was handed over to Sonadanga Model Police Station for further legal action.

item.title: President urges farmers to form central body to protect interests
item.description:
President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir on Sunday called upon farmers to form a central organization at the national level to ensure their overall development and protect interests, irrespective of party affiliation, opinion or path.
The president made the call as an eight-member delegation of the Bangladesh Farmers Association, led by its President Md Siddiqur Rahman Kul Moyez, paid a courtesy call on him at Bangabhaban.
The president said farmers are the real and finest people of the country. "They are the warriors who build the country. To honour and inspire these farmers, an initiative will be taken to introduce the President's Agriculture Award for new innovations and outstanding contributions in the agriculture sector," he said.
He also assured the farmers of all-out cooperation and advised them to communicate at the highest level, and called for turning the interests of farmers into a movement.
"Agriculture remains the most progressive sector of the country. Due to hard work of farmers, the development of new high-yielding varieties and agricultural technologies, and the proper use of technology, crop production has increased manifold," he said.
He added that farmers do not engage in corruption rather they contribute to the progress of society and the state. The president called for developing effective marketing system so that agricultural products and crops can easily reach consumers and farmers receive fair price.
"The incumbent government has introduced a new scheme for ensuring fair prices for agricultural products and the development of farmers, and Tk3,000 crore has already been allocated," he observed.
"The government has also waived agricultural loans, including interest, of up to Tk10,000 for farmers," he said, assuring that initiatives would be taken to reduce interest rates on loans taken from NGOs.
At the time, he highlighted various initiatives taken by the government for the development of agriculture and farmers including arranging agricultural loans at low interest.

item.title: CUET protests enter sixth day as teachers hold sit-in
item.description:
The movement demanding the reinstatement of former Chittagong University of Engineering and Technology (CUET) Vice-Chancellor Prof Dr Abu Sadat Muhammad Sayem entered its sixth day Sunday, with students observing a complete shutdown and teachers holding a sit-in.
The CUET Teachers’ Association held the sit-in in front of the vice-chancellor’s residence from 11am to 1pm, while students brought out a procession and chanted slogans demanding Prof Sayem’s reinstatement.
The students rejected the newly appointed vice-chancellor on Saturday by displaying red cards. The CUET Teachers’ Association and Officers’ Association have also joined the movement, resulting in the suspension of all academic and administrative activities.
Students planned a sit-in at the university’s main gate and a street play and other programs on Sunday. They said they would not return to classes until Prof Sayem is reinstated.
On September 21, the government issued a notification removing Prof Sayem and appointing Prof Dr Sheikh Shariful Alam of Khulna University of Engineering and Technology (KUET) as CUET vice-chancellor.

item.title: Cox’s Bazar’s tourism boom comes at a cost
item.description:
Millions of tourists flock to Cox’s Bazar each year to enjoy its iconic sea beach, but growing commercial activity, traffic congestion, waste and inadequate facilities are increasingly affecting the visitor experience.
At the Laboni, Sugandha and Kalatali points, rows of temporary shops, street vendors, beach bikes, horses, photographers and other commercial activities have become a familiar sight.
For some visitors, the growing presence of vendors and businesses is taking away from the tranquillity of the beach.
“Within a few minutes of entering the beach, different vendors start approaching us,” said Lovely Akter, who visited Cox’s Bazar from Dhaka with her family.
“We came to enjoy the sea, but we have to listen to business offers repeatedly,” she said.
Tourist couple Sohel Mazhar and Shiuli, who travelled from Rajshahi, also complained about the quality and cost of services.
Millions of tourists come to Cox’s Bazar to enjoy the sea beach, but services have not improved at the same pace, they said. Commercial activities are everywhere, and prices often seem excessive. The authorities need to pay greater attention to this.
During peak tourism seasons, traffic congestion is a regular problem in Kalatali, Sugandha and Jhautala. Unplanned parking, footpath encroachment and increasing traffic volumes make movement difficult for tourists and local residents alike.
Tourism stakeholders say the growth in visitor numbers has not been matched by adequate improvements in infrastructure and urban management.
Environmentalists are also concerned about the impact of unregulated activities and increasing tourist pressure on the beach ecosystem.
Dipak Sharma Dipu, president of the Cox’s Bazar Forest and Environment Journalists’ Council, said the sea, sandy beach and natural environment are the destination’s most important assets.
“Unplanned commercial activities, noise pollution, plastic waste and other uncontrolled activities are gradually damaging the beach environment,” he said.
Plastic bottles, food wrappers and other waste are frequently found on different parts of the beach, he said, adding that such waste not only affects the area’s beauty but could also pose a threat to marine biodiversity.
Local businesses say tourism-related commercial activities are also an important source of livelihood for thousands of people.
Mohammad Abdullah, manager of Beach Bangla Tourism in Cox’s Bazar, said vendors, small traders, photographers, transport workers and hotel and restaurant employees all depend on the tourism economy.
“Thousands of people depend on tourism for their livelihoods,” he said. “The solution is not to stop business activities, but to ensure that they are properly regulated and managed.”
Tourism stakeholders say designated commercial zones, improved waste management, better parking facilities and long-term traffic management could help balance commercial interests with the needs of tourists and the environment.
Moukhim Khan, general secretary of the Kalatali-Marine Drive Road Hotel-Motel Owners’ Association, said Cox’s Bazar needs better facilities and international-standard events to attract tourists throughout the year.
“Regular government-organised fairs and other events could help attract tourists year-round,” he said. “At the same time, the quality of tourist services must be improved.”
Abu Morshed Chowdhury Khoka, president of Cox’s Bazar Civil Society, said environmental protection must remain a priority alongside tourism development.
“The natural beauty of Cox’s Bazar is important not only for tourists but also for the national economy,” he said. “If the openness, aesthetic appeal and natural environment of the beach are not protected, it could eventually affect tourists’ interest in the destination.”
Cox’s Bazar Deputy Commissioner Md Abdul Mannan said the government has taken initiatives to promote sustainable tourism and improve tourist safety, cleanliness and modern facilities.
“A master plan is being prepared to develop sustainable tourism and attract foreign tourists,” he said.
He said initiatives were also being taken to restore order on the beach, ensure cleanliness, remove illegal encroachments and improve tourist safety.
Meanwhile, a three-day tourism fair has been organized in Cox’s Bazar to mark World Tourism Day, which promotes sustainable, environmentally friendly and people-centred tourism.
For Cox’s Bazar, the message is particularly relevant. The city’s tourism economy depends fundamentally on the natural beauty of its coastline. Managing commercial activity, protecting the environment and improving public services will therefore remain central to the destination’s long-term tourism prospects.
As the number of visitors continues to grow, the challenge for Cox’s Bazar is to ensure that tourism development does not come at the expense of the very natural environment that attracts tourists in the first place.

item.title: Schoolgirl hacked to death: Accused sentenced to death after 19 years
item.description:
A Dhaka court on Sunday sentenced Rezaul Islam to death for killing seventh-grade student Mahmuda Akter Roxi in Ashulia, Savar, in 2007 after she rejected his marriage proposal.
Judge Md Humayun Kabir of the 3rd Additional District and Sessions Judge’s Court in Dhaka delivered the verdict. The court also directed the relevant police superintendent to take measures to arrest the fugitive convict and enforce the sentence.
Bench assistant Md Aminur Rahman confirmed the matter.
According to the case details and court sources, Rezaul proposed marriage to Roxi, a fatherless orphan student from Ashulia, on March 28, 2007. After she rejected the proposal, Rezaul allegedly threatened and intimidated her.
On the morning of April 2, 2007, Rezaul entered Roxi’s room and repeatedly struck her on the head with a spade. The attack fractured her skull into 3 pieces and exposed her brain.
Roxi was rescued in critical condition and taken to Dhaka Medical College Hospital, where she died that night while undergoing treatment.
Following the incident, Roxi’s maternal cousin Nurul Islam Babu filed a murder case with Ashulia police station.
After completing the investigation, Ashulia Police Station Sub-Inspector Alim Uddin submitted a charge sheet to the court on July 4, 2007, naming Rezaul Islam as the sole accused.
On March 4, 2008, the court framed charges against Rezaul and ordered the trial to begin.
During the trial, the court recorded testimony from 12 witnesses, including the complainant, the doctor who conducted the autopsy, the magistrate who recorded the accused’s confessional statement, the investigating officer and local eyewitnesses.
After reviewing the evidence and testimony, the court found the charges against Rezaul proved beyond reasonable doubt and sentenced him to death.
Rezaul has been absconding after obtaining bail and failing to appear before the court. The court directed the relevant police superintendent to take necessary measures to arrest him and enforce the sentence.

item.title: Gunfire, looting, vandalism in midnight Dhaka rampage
item.description:
An armed group arriving in pickup trucks stormed a property development near Dhaka’s ECB Chattar area, allegedly opening fire, assaulting workers and looting valuables before vandalising buildings, including popular content creator Salman Muqtadir’s Brownfish Studio, in an attack police say stemmed from a dispute over around 35 kathas of land.
The Saturday night assault at New Gini Properties in South Manikdi has since escalated into a wider controversy over law and order after Salman publicly challenged Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed over the police response and the minister’s initial assertion that the content creator had not filed a case.
Police said on Sunday night that four people, including alleged organiser Shahriar Mahmud, had been arrested.
Five spent cartridges, pellets and locally made weapons were recovered from the scene, Cantonment Police Station Officer-in-Charge Mohammad Gias Uddin told Dhaka Tribune.
A case has been filed against 13 named suspects and 150-200 unidentified people over the attack.
The complaint accuses the group of entering the property armed with firearms and sharp weapons, firing to create panic, assaulting workers and security personnel, vandalising the project office and looting Tk25 lakh.
Police and the government, however, have described a land dispute -- rather than a confirmed extortion attempt against Salman -- as the apparent trigger.
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said preliminary information showed that New Gini Properties and a retired senior military officer had been locked in a dispute over approximately 35 kathas of land in Manikdi.
A group allegedly acting for the other side went to the property at night in an attempt to take possession, damaging structures on the site, including the facility housing Salman’s studio, the minister said.
Salman himself has said he did not believe he was necessarily the intended target, but argued that the circumstances surrounding the dispute did not diminish the broader question of public safety.
The case filed by New Gini Properties director Md Saiful Islam Bhuiyan paints a picture of an organised armed assault.
According to the complaint, the attackers entered the project at around 11:20pm carrying shotguns, revolvers, chapatis, ramdas, daggers, iron rods and sticks.
It alleges that around 50 rounds were fired to spread panic, sending workers and security guards scrambling for safety.
Site engineer Md Parvez was allegedly assaulted, while security guard Syed Nazrul Islam was also attacked when he intervened.
The attackers allegedly fired another 10 rounds towards the main gate before entering the project office, vandalising it and breaking open a locker containing Tk25 lakh intended for construction-material purchases.
The allegations in the case have not yet been established in court.
Residents described hearing sustained gunfire, shouting and vandalism.
Munni Akter, who lives nearby, said residents were too frightened to leave their homes.
She said she saw people arriving in four or five pickup trucks before hearing gunshots, screaming and sounds of vandalism for nearly an hour.
Construction worker Sohel said workers had been sleeping when a large group stormed the site.
He alleged that CCTV cameras were smashed and workers were intimidated before their mobile phones and cash were taken.
Another worker, Muhin, estimated that 200-300 people were involved and said 50-60 gunshots could be heard. Workers alleged that 30-40 mobile phones and cash were taken from people at the site.
The attack initially drew national attention after Salman posted videos showing the devastation inside Brownfish Studio.
Furniture and equipment had been smashed, while Salman alleged that CCTV cameras and the surveillance server were also taken.
In his first response, Salman suggested the attackers may have been targeting the property owner rather than him and referred to what he had heard about possible extortion.
He subsequently broadened his criticism to the country’s law-and-order situation.
That prompted a response from Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed, who called Salman’s allegation portraying the BNP as an extortionist party “sweeping.”
The minister said Salman had himself acknowledged that nobody had directly demanded money from him and argued that allegations should be backed by specific complaints.
Salahuddin also initially questioned whether Salman had filed a case.
Salman responded hours later, saying the minister had been given incorrect information.
He said he had gone to Cantonment Police Station on the night of the attack and remained there until around 4am while the case was filed.
“I, and the entire nation, ought to be asking you why the case wasn’t filed earlier,” Salman said in his response.
He argued that the central issue was not whether the underlying dispute involved land, extortion or people affiliated with any political party, but whether the state could protect citizens from an armed attack.
“The issue was safety and security,” he said.
Salman has acknowledged that the attackers may not have known his studio was located on the property.
“Those who carried out the attack likely didn’t know this was my property,” he said after the incident.
He said he believed the underlying target was connected to the property dispute and that his studio was caught in the middle.
Police have offered a broadly similar preliminary assessment.
Cantonment police said the dispute involved New Gini Properties and a retired major general and that Salman’s studio was damaged during the resulting attack.
New Gini Properties Chairman Nazim Uddin Molla, however, told Dhaka Tribune that he had previously received threats and demands for extortion.
“They came on Saturday night and vandalised everything,” he said, alleging that the group had caused trouble in the area before.
No evidence establishing that allegation was available to Dhaka Tribune.
Cantonment police initially reported three arrests, but OC Mohammad Gias Uddin later told Dhaka Tribune that four people were in custody.
They included Shahriar Mahmud, whom police described as the alleged organiser, along with Md Mamun, Aslam and Munna.
Police said the men had been hired to participate in the attack and that operations were continuing to identify and arrest others.
The case names Shahriar Mahmud as the prime accused and alleges that the attack was carried out at his instigation and direction.
With competing claims surrounding the ownership dispute and allegations of extortion yet to be established, investigators must now determine who organised and financed an armed operation that witnesses say brought hundreds of people into a residential area of the capital, why firearms were used and whether the assault could have been prevented.
For Salman, those questions go beyond the destruction of his studio.
He said he could rebuild what he had lost, but argued that the greater concern was what an attack of this scale meant for people without his resources or public platform.

item.title: A global stage, a missed opportunity
item.description:
The UN General Assembly offered Prime Minister Tarique Rahman an opportunity to transcend the country’s petty political factionalism and showcase Bangladesh as a nation capable of playing a leading role on the global stage.
While this opportunity arises annually, the political transformation following the 2024 uprising lent this particular session added significance for Bangladesh.
The question now arises: Did Prime Minister Tarique Rahman make the most of this opportunity? Or did he simply follow the conventional script -- extolling his own party, vilifying opponents, and delivering a bland, bureaucratic speech on geopolitical issues that carefully avoided taking a firm stand?
It became evident right at the start of the speech that the PM would not chart a new course.
Although the nation is 55 years old, he indulged in nostalgia, recalling only the speeches delivered from that very podium by his father, the late President Ziaur Rahman, and his mother, former Prime Minister Khaleda Zia.
He could also have acknowledged that Sheikh Mujibur Rahman delivered the first-ever speech in Bangla from that same platform in 1974. Doing so would not have undermined his standing as the country’s elected representative.
Yet, no matter how grand the stage, the country’s narrow political climate leaves little room for such magnanimity.
Even when standing on the global stage, Bangladeshi leaders struggle to break free from the political divisions they leave behind at home. There have been precedents for this, and this instance was no exception.
The PM blamed the past, labelled his ousted political rivals “fascists,” and presented his party’s agenda as a blueprint for development.
It was expected that he would speak of the country’s return to the path of democracy, and it was hardly surprising that he praised the February election.
However, when the domestic practice of branding the ousted Awami League as “fascist” is exported to the global stage, it effectively amounts to painting a large segment of the nation’s population as the “enemy.”
It would have signalled a new kind of politics had he spoken solely of progress rather than portraying a fractured nation by assigning blame to others.
At one point in the speech, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman stated: “By ensuring the political and economic empowerment of the people, we aim to establish a prosperous, self-reliant, and democratic welfare state -- a nation where everyone, regardless of political affiliation, religion, or race, can live securely and safely with equal rights, honour, and dignity.”
There is no doubt that these words sound appealing to everyone.
However, it would hardly be surprising if these sentiments seemed hollow when certain party activists and supporters live in fear of arrest while facing fabricated charges, languish in prison for months without trial, or, branded as “accomplices” while being subjected to attacks, handed over to the police, and jailed on false accusations.
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman touched upon several significant issues in his speech, including migration, the impact of climate change, artificial intelligence, the Rohingya crisis, the volatile global situation, and the UN’s development goals.
In each instance, the government’s programs or achievements were highlighted. In some areas, particularly regarding the avoidance of geopolitical conflict, he advocated peace efforts and disarmament.
These are standard topics in UN politics; statements made by developing nations on these matters are often heard by others but usually forgotten before they even leave UN headquarters.
However, it is worth examining how the PM’s own publicity team is attempting to present his speech to the nation.
While briefing journalists in New York, Mahdi Amin, a spokesperson for the Prime Minister’s Office, described Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s address to the UN General Assembly as “historic and groundbreaking.”
Mahdi Amin stated that, through this speech, Bangladesh had “created a new history.”
What is this new history? Reading Amin’s remarks, it appears that he views the rare occurrence of three members of the same family addressing the UN as heads of government as the “historic” event.
It was not merely the family connection, however, but the glorification of the leader that appeared to be the government spokesperson’s primary focus.
“Through this speech, the world witnessed how a head of government transforms into a true statesman,” Amin said.
He reminded the nation that the PM did not confine himself to matters concerning Bangladesh alone, he also spoke about global peace and the rights of the freedom-seeking people of Palestine, and even offered counsel to the United Nations itself.
“He presented a concrete roadmap to world leaders on how the UN can play a robust role in restoring peace, prosperity, and unity across the globe,” Mahdi Amin said at a press conference.
There is no doubt that Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s speech touched upon these issues.
However, there is room for disagreement over whether these remarks were truly “historic” or “statesmanlike.”
First, heads of government from Bangladesh have always spoken about Palestinian rights when addressing the UN.
Nor is this unique to Bangladesh; leaders from most nations speak of peace and prosperity and express a desire to see the UN play a stronger and more effective role.
These are standard talking points for developing nations at international conferences.
Second, one could not merely disagree with, but vehemently dispute, the spokesperson’s claim that Prime Minister Tarique Rahman “presented a concrete roadmap to world leaders” on how the UN could play a robust role.
While Prime Minister Tarique Rahman certainly spoke eloquently about the UN’s role and what is expected of it, can those remarks truly be described as a “roadmap?”
The prime minister was correct in stating that, in the era of globalization, conflict in one part of the world can trigger unrest and economic disaster elsewhere.
He spoke of establishing bilateral or multilateral relations among disputing states based on “equality, fairness, mutual interest, and respect for dignity,” points with which few would disagree.
“Bangladesh envisions the UN as the focal point for establishing a cooperative global society that respects each other’s independence and sovereignty,” the PM said in his speech.
These are all fine sentiments. But where is the “roadmap” for the UN here? A roadmap would typically contain specific proposals and outline concrete steps.
These remarks are undoubtedly significant, particularly in the context of post-2024 Bangladesh-India relations. However, such sentiments are not new on the global stage, and all too often remain nothing more than rhetoric once the speech concludes.
Had the prime minister wished, he could have presented concrete proposals for reforming the UN Security Council or addressing the crisis in development funding.
Regarding the Rohingya crisis, instead of merely seeking international cooperation, he could have offered specific proposals grounded in reality; he could even have announced unilateral measures to reinforce Bangladesh’s commitment to the disarmament process.
The speech would have been truly “historic” or “groundbreaking” had it put forward proposals aimed at playing a leading role in resolving problems rather than simply positioning the nation as a victim.
As it stands, however, it appears that the address amounted to little more than a routine bureaucratic exercise of reading from prepared talking points.
Sabir Mustafa is the former head of BBC Bangla and is currently working as a freelance journalist and podcaster. Views expressed are the author’s own.

item.title: Police arrest mastermind in Salman Muqtadir studio attack

item.description:
NEPAL-FLOODS/

Heavy rain and storms have triggered floods and landslides that killed 56 people in India, while in Nepal, 14 have died and another 11 are missing, with authorities there warning on Sunday that more flash floods are possible.

India's northern state of Uttar Pradesh recorded 66.5 mm of rain between 25 September and the morning of 27 September, compared with a normal 7.6 mm for the period, Hrishikesh Bhaskar Yashod, the state's relief commissioner, said on Sunday.

Authorities are carrying out rescue operations in waterlogged areas and distributing relief, while officials have been told to assess crop damage and provide compensation.

In addition to the 56 deaths, 46 people have been injured and more than 1,000 houses have been damaged.

Nepali authorities warned of possible flash floods in 49 of the country's 77 districts, with more than half facing high flood or flash-flood risks as water levels in major rivers and tributaries continued to rise.

Shanti Mahat, a spokesperson for the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, said Rasuwa and Nuwakot, areas hit by last month's deadly floods that killed more than 1,450 people and left thousands still missing, should remain "alert" but were not currently considered high-risk areas.

item.title: Trump expects new Iran talks despite rejecting deal offer
item.description:
USA-TRUMP/

US President Donald Trump said Sunday that he expects talks with Iran to resume in the coming week, despite his rejection of a truce proposal put forward by Tehran.

Iranian officials brought with them to the UN General Assembly in New York a plan for a seven-day truce followed by the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz shipping channel.

Trump dismissed the plan and has mused on resuming full-scale air strikes on Iranian targets, but he told the news platform Axios that he expects negotiations to resume.

"They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make," Trump told Axios. "It is what we would have maybe agreed to a year ago."

"They overplayed their hand," Trump said, in the interview published Sunday.

Citing sources familiar with the matter, Axios reported that indirect talks between Washington and Tehran could take place as early as Monday.

On Sunday, Iran was still standing by its conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, leaving the Gulf front of the Middle East war locked in a stalemate, while fighting rages in Yemen.

How Trump's diplomatic week exposed the limits of his power

'We will not back down'

Hormuz is a key chokepoint for the world's energy supplies and is now central to the conflict between Washington and Tehran, which was started nearly seven months ago when the US and Israel launched a wave of strikes against Iran.

Iran's plan called for a cessation of all hostilities in the Middle East, including in Lebanon, according to Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, and a return to the conditions in an earlier ceasefire deal that fell apart.

That agreement, which collapsed during fighting over Hormuz, called for the release of frozen Iranian assets, the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil and an end to the US naval blockade.

"Our conditions are clear, and any move toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz is contingent upon these conditions being fulfilled. We will not back down from them," Araghchi said on Sunday, state broadcaster IRIB reported.

"We have never closed the door to diplomacy or negotiations, but at the same time, we have never backed down from our rights."

Washington's ambassador to the UN, Mike Waltz, accused Tehran of demanding too much in exchange for a return to the negotiating table.

"This was, I think, a pretty cynical attempt to put something on the table that they knew was unacceptable. To ask for the release of the blockade, the sanctions, international sanctions and access to billions in assets, just to talk," he told NBC News in an interview broadcast Sunday.

"I think it's kind of common sense that the president doesn't have a lot of confidence this time after we just tried a few months ago."

Iran's Revolutionary Guards meanwhile said that they seized an American submersible drone on Sunday in the Strait of Hormuz.

It said the underwater vehicle was being used "for espionage purposes", adding that it was "now in the hands of the force's specialists for data recovery".

Trump rejects Iranian proposal to open Hormuz and end fighting

'Tool for pressure'

Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding in June aimed at ending the war, reopening the strait and launching talks on Iran's nuclear programme.

But the deal broke down shortly afterwards when Iran fired on commercial ships in Hormuz that it accused of deviating from its approved route through the waterway.

Iran requires ships to obtain authorization before passage, citing security and sovereignty reasons.

Ships that refuse to comply are regularly targeted, while the United States sporadically bombs Iranian coastal areas in retaliation.

Araghchi said at the UN that Iran has conveyed to the United States, through Qatar, a concrete seven-day plan, adding: "The choice now rests with the United States."

Hossein Mohebi, a spokesman for Iran's Revolutionary Guards, was quoted by Tasnim news agency as saying: "We will not cease punishing the US until Iran's seven conditions are met."

Mohebi had told AFP in an exclusive interview on Tuesday that ending hostilities in Yemen was also among Tehran's demands.
